title: A Reproducible Synthetic Benchmark and Deterministic Validator for Evaluating LLM‑Driven NetOps: A Paired Confirmatory Comparison of a GVR Pipeline and Single‑Pass Generation
abstract: We preregistered, executed, and archived a sealed synthetic benchmark and deterministic validator to compare a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline against a frozen single‑pass LLM (declared: gpt-5-mini) on N=300 intent→configuration tasks. The paired design used a shared initial candidate per task (both conditions reuse the same generation) and allowed at most one automatic repair call for the guarded condition. Execution accounting: planned_episode_count=600, completed_episode_count=600, model_calls_used=301 (300 shared initial calls + 1 repair); authoritative raw provider traces: execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d). Results: baseline 299/300 passes (0.9967), guarded 300/300 passes (1.0); paired contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; paired difference = 0.00333; paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The preregistered target effect (0.10) was unattainable given the observed ceiling baseline and the constrained repair budget. We (a) report where the single repair provider trace and the unique discordant pair can be deterministically located within the archived raw_results container (see Results), (b) disclose which preregistered secondary estimands were not executed and why, and (c) provide artifact‑grounded recommendations for future confirmatory tests.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to automate NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation, change planning, and remediation. Prior empirical work shows LLMs can produce plausible configuration fragments but often make syntax, topology, or semantic errors; guarded pipelines that combine generation with deterministic verification and localized repair have been proposed to reduce operational misconfiguration risk. Despite prototypes and case studies, the community lacks standardized, machine‑checkable benchmarks that pair explicit intent tasks with deterministic validator semantics and sealed preregistration for confirmatory comparisons. To address this gap we preregistered and executed study ac-2026-003-prereg-v1: (1) a deterministic synthetic intent→configuration task bank, (2) a snapshot deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, v5.0) that enforces required sequence and workflow constraints, and (3) a paired comparison of a guarded GVR pipeline versus a frozen single‑pass generator using a shared‑initial candidate design. The preregistered research question was: under fixed seeds and a constrained repair budget (≤1 repair call per failed candidate), does a GVR pipeline increase the per‑task validator pass rate relative to a frozen single‑pass LLM?
sections.related_work: Surveys and reviews document rapid growth in LLM‑for‑NetOps research and consistently identify verification, hallucination, and prompt‑injection as critical deployment challenges [https://openalex.org/W4406137434, https://openalex.org/W4415071524, https://openalex.org/W4402742293]. Empirical studies demonstrate that out‑of‑the‑box LLMs can synthesize router and device configurations but commonly require verifier assistance or human adjudication to reach operational correctness [https://openalex.org/W4388629193; 10.1145/3626111.3628194]. Generate–validate–repair and tool‑assisted prompting have improved correctness in focused prototypes [https://openalex.org/W4404652946], yet dataset scope and reproducibility are often limited. Security analyses of prompt injection and adversarial prompts underscore the need for guarded architectures and deterministic validators in operational workflows [https://openalex.org/W4405181600, https://openalex.org/W4388886073]. Our contribution is a sealed, archived proof‑of‑concept benchmark and a confirmatory paired run tying a deterministic snapshot validator to an automated repair trigger under a tightly specified retry and budget policy, with full artifact archival to support deterministic reproduction or extension.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design. We preregistered ac-2026-003-prereg-v1 before execution (preregistration SHA‑256 = a05938dad3a61e1f4aae518bcb42244009b0403a18387ceeff4be1d86ce87765). Primary hypothesis H1: the GVR pipeline produces a higher per‑task validator pass rate than a frozen single‑pass generator on N=300 paired tasks (two‑sided α=0.05). The plan fixed task generation, validator semantics, inclusion/exclusion rules, missingness treatment, analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1), and repair budget (≤1 repair call per failed candidate). The registered execution contract specified a shared_initial generation (one generation used as baseline and as the guarded pipeline's initial candidate) to isolate repair value. The preregistration lists secondary/exploratory estimands (per_task_failure_rate_guarded, per_task_failure_rate_baseline, effect_size_Cohen_h_equivalent_for_paired_proportions) and exploratory analyses; all design choices are archived.

Task bank. A deterministic generator produced 300 synthetic tasks partitioned into four intent clusters (reachability, isolation, ACLs, route policies; 75 tasks each). Each task encodes initial_state, expected_final_state, allowed_fields, workflow_policies, difficulty label, and a required_sequence that the validator enforces. Tasks span device counts 3–50 and use abstracted multi‑vendor device models; no private customer data are included. Representative manifests and the full task_manifest.jsonl are archived (execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 = 062b80216e49a2919ebf8debd75cf02fffcfd752b5b253e5a11c0701ca853097).

Validator and scoring rule. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0) implements full_intent_constraint_validation as a stateless snapshot checker: it (a) parses candidate commands into canonical field operations, (b) enforces required_sequence and workflow_policies (ordering, mutual‑exclusion, group constraints), (c) applies allowed_fields and preserves unspecified state when requested, (d) computes the implied final_state, and (e) returns a binary pass/fail with diagnostic violation codes and a per‑task validator trace. Per‑task scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/*.json) contain normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, validation_before/after traces, and validator.valid flags. The validator was expressly selected to provide machine‑checkable binary outcomes fit for confirmatory inference.

Modeling, orchestration, and determinism. The declared model was gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820) executed via adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1 with provider = "openai_responses". Invocation parameters were fixed (max_output_tokens=2000; maximum_attempts_per_call=1; reasoning_effort="minimal"; temperature=null). The orchestration used deterministic sampling semantics recorded in the provider traces; the authoritative per‑call provider traces are archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d). Reproducing identical hosted outputs therefore requires replaying these archived traces or access to the identical provider model release and invocation semantics documented in execution/model_configuration.json.

Analysis plan. The primary estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline on N=300 paired binary outcomes. The preregistered inferential test is the exact McNemar two‑sided test; we also compute a paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Missingness and sensitivity treatments (complete_pair_primary and failure_as_zero) were preregistered.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and provider audit. The execution manifest reports: started_at_utc = 2026-08-29T12:41:43.384097+00:00, completed_at_utc = 2026-08-29T13:07:38.995000+00:00, planned_episode_count = 600, completed_episode_count = 600, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 301, artifact_hash_count = 2108. Provider_call_audit (deterministic_reconciliation.json) records hosted_model_call_event_count = 301 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1}, i.e., the guarded pipeline invoked the registered repair stage exactly once across N=300 tasks. The authoritative provider traces are archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d).

Primary confirmatory outcomes. Aggregated counts (analysis/condition_summary.csv SHA‑256 = 55eacb88c64f29dc9c5ce1ca7079eca9b4a94b5d3a2970dae019a81a1decf73b): baseline_success_count = 299/300 (0.9966667); guarded_success_count = 300/300 (1.0). The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = 3421adb52d5791a979397368165fc2062e6b9a4a771ce49c0bcac80b02215d55) is: n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI (percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.00, 0.01]. All analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle.

Location of the single repair provider trace and discordant pair identifier. The single repair invocation and its paired outcome are archived in the authoritative provider trace container execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d). Because stage_counts indicate exactly one record with stage="repair", auditors can deterministically locate the repair trace and the discordant pair identifier by parsing execution/raw_results.jsonl for records whose stage field equals "repair"; that record contains the provider_call metadata including the pair_id and the full per‑call provider trace. The execution manifest and deterministic_reconciliation.json provide cross‑references to validate that this is the unique repair record for the study. We deliberately present the raw_results container SHA here so auditors can verify integrity before extracting the unique repair entry.

Preregistered secondary estimands and execution status. The preregistration listed exploratory/secondary estimands including per_task_failure_rate_guarded, per_task_failure_rate_baseline, and effect_size_Cohen_h_equivalent_for_paired_proportions. The archived analysis artifacts show no populated preregistered secondary_results (analysis secondary_results = []). The simple per‑condition failure rates are nevertheless reported above (baseline and guarded success/failure counts). The preregistered effect_size_Cohen_h_equivalent_for_paired_proportions and other specified exploratory effect‑size computations were not executed as formal secondary_results by the registered executor because the observed contingency margins (baseline ≈0.997, guarded =1.0) produced a ceiling scenario with only one discordant pair; under these arithmetic conditions such effect‑size computations are uninformative, and the registered confirmatory executor produced no additional secondary estimand outputs. We therefore (a) report the observed marginal counts and (b) note that the preregistered exploratory estimands remain executable on the archived artifacts should future auditors wish to recompute them under alternative missingness or treatment assumptions.

Interpretation and arithmetic ceiling effect. The exact McNemar two‑sided p depends only on the discordant counts n10 and n01. With n10=1 and n01=0 the exact two‑sided p reported by the preregistered executor is 1.0; this reflects the near absence of discordant pairs rather than an analytic error. Practically, the preregistered target effect of 0.10 is arithmetically unattainable given the observed baseline margin (≈0.9967): the maximum possible paired gain with these margins is 1/300 ≈ 0.00333 (the observed difference). Consequently, the bootstrap percentile CI [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) provides a more informative summary of practical uncertainty than the two‑sided p in this ceiling context.
sections.discussion:
Scope and operational meaning of the null finding. The confirmatory null applies strictly to the sealed design: synthetic deterministic tasks, a shared initial candidate, a snapshot deterministic validator, and a constrained repair budget (≤1 repair call). Under these constrained conditions the guarded GVR pipeline rarely differed from the baseline because the shared initial generator already satisfied the validator in 299/300 cases; therefore the guarded pipeline could improve only once. This outcome does not imply GVR architectures are generically unhelpful; rather, it quantifies that when generator quality is near ceiling and repair budgets are tightly constrained, localized repair yields negligible marginal benefit.

Artifact‑grounded recommendations. The archived evidence supports concrete modifications to make repair efficacy measurable in future confirmatory runs: increase task difficulty or include adversarial seeds to raise initial failure rates (the execution logs show 299/300 initial successes); permit iterative or larger repair budgets per failed candidate (stage_counts indicate repair=1 here, effectively inert); allow multiple independent initial generations per task when evaluating selection or reranking strategies rather than repair efficacy; adopt stateful/emulation validators that model ordered side effects and temporal execution; and include explicit adversarial prompt/test cases to exercise prompt‑hardening defenses. Each recommendation maps directly to observed execution facts and to per‑task diagnostics archived in the bundle.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: the shared‑initial design controls generator variance but does not evaluate multi‑sample baselines or alternative selection strategies; minimal repair engagement limits within‑study contrasts. Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces snapshot intent constraints but omits vendor CLI idiosyncrasies and in‑flight temporal behavior; some real‑world failure modes may be missed. External validity: tasks are synthetic (3–50 devices, abstracted multi‑vendor) and only one declared model (gpt-5-mini) and validator (v5.0) were evaluated; results do not generalize to production networks or other models without further experiments. Conclusion validity: the small number of discordant outcomes (n10=1) leaves subgroup and failure‑mode inference underpowered.

Operational implications and reuse. For practitioners: when generator correctness under deterministic sampling is already near ceiling and repair budgets are constrained, guarded repair mechanisms provide minimal marginal gains. In settings with lower generator reliability, adversarial inputs, or relaxed repair policies (iterative repairs, multi‑generation selection), GVR pipelines are more likely to yield measurable operational benefit. We release the preregistration, execution manifest, raw responses, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts so practitioners and researchers can instantiate harder settings or alternate analysis treatments without rebuilding baseline infrastructure.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered, executed, and archived a sealed synthetic NetOps benchmark and deterministic validator and ran a paired confirmatory comparison of a guarded GVR pipeline versus a frozen single‑pass gpt-5-mini generator on N=300 intent→configuration tasks. Both approaches achieved near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300; guarded 300/300). The preregistered hypothesis that GVR would produce a materially higher pass rate (target 0.10) was not supported; this null result is explained by a ceiling baseline and minimal repair engagement (stage_counts show shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1). We provide artifact‑grounded recommendations and archive the authoritative artifacts (including execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 0d841d29...) so the community can extend the benchmark with harder tasks, iterative repair budgets, multi‑generation baselines, and multi‑model comparisons that can demonstrate when GVR pipelines yield measurable operational value.

limitations: Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces snapshot intent constraints but does not model temporal in‑flight execution dynamics, vendor CLI idiosyncrasies, or asynchronous side effects.

External validity: tasks are synthetic (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models) and may not capture production heterogeneity; findings do not imply equivalent performance on real production networks or private customer data.

Ceiling effect: near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300, guarded 300/300) reduce sensitivity to detect the preregistered target effect (0.10) and therefore constrain confirmatory inference about practical superiority of GVR under broader conditions.
Model and scope limits: only gpt-5-mini was declared and evaluated; findings do not generalize to other model families or sizes without further experiments.

GVR engagement: the guarded repair stage executed only once across N=300 tasks (provider recorded stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1), so the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline; this pipeline inactivity constrains conclusions about repair effectiveness under alternative trigger policies or larger repair budgets.
Failure‑mode analysis: only one discordant outcome occurred (n10=1), leaving exploratory failure clustering and subgroup inference underpowered and inconclusive.

Reproducibility caveat: reproducing identical hosted model outputs may require access to the same hosted model release and provider invocation semantics recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and the per‑call provider traces archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29...).

Artifact‑inclusion note: the exact per‑task artifacts that contain the single repair provider trace and the single discordant episode identifier are present in the archived execution bundle (execution manifest and execution/raw_results.jsonl) and are authoritative for auditors.
